rationales.quote: How do you onboard a city?
rationales.explanation: Charles asks about the company’s customer-onboarding and sales process for cities.

rationales.quote: How do you onboard a city?
rationales.explanation: Charles repeats the onboarding question to clarify how cities become customers.

rationales.quote: how do you get all the information?
rationales.explanation: He probes the practical data-collection requirements for setting up the product.

rationales.quote: Do they have to, do these ever have to go through any like procurement or competitive bid or can you, can you just like, sole source buy this?
rationales.explanation: He asks whether government procurement rules could affect the sales motion.

rationales.quote: How hard would it be to get the sub 5,000 people towns to be basically self-serve?
rationales.explanation: He probes whether the smallest towns can be served through a scalable, low-touch model.

rationales.quote: Yeah, it doesn't work. It doesn't work otherwise, right?
rationales.explanation: Charles states that serving these towns is not viable without a self-serve approach.

rationales.quote: this business works well if your marketing presence and energy is focused on getting the towns that are worth your time
rationales.explanation: He sees a viable sales strategy in concentrating founder-led effort on higher-value towns.

rationales.quote: you've gotta have a different engine that's probably more like a marketing engine that gets all of these towns that are below the line for you such that you can pick them up with less effort
rationales.explanation: He identifies a scalable marketing engine for smaller towns as necessary to avoid inefficient founder-led selling.

rationales.quote: I don't know how you get to the revenue number that you probably need without at least getting the beginnings of that marketing engine self-serve for the small
rationales.explanation: He is uncertain that the company can reach the required revenue without proving scalable acquisition of small towns.

rationales.quote: you know the customer
rationales.explanation: Charles believes Nichole’s customer knowledge will help her close larger towns.

rationales.quote: there's like a temptation to do that 'cause they're gonna wanna talk to you 'cause you're the expert
rationales.explanation: He flags the risk that small-town customers will pull the founder into inefficient, high-touch selling.

rationales.quote: You don't need to get many grants for that to pay for itself.
rationales.explanation: He views the grants automation as economically compelling because a small number of grants could cover its cost.

rationales.quote: What happens?
rationales.explanation: Charles asks what downstream effects the system identifies when municipal code changes.

rationales.quote: I'm gonna say yes because I think I'm gonna like the answers
rationales.explanation: He says his narrow yes was based on expecting the founder’s responses to diligence questions to demonstrate a workable relationship.

rationales.quote: how you think about deal size, growing over time
rationales.explanation: He asks how monetization and customer deal size can expand over time.

rationales.quote: How do we scale you, since you are like such a unique asset for the company?
rationales.explanation: He probes how the company can reduce dependence on Nichole as a uniquely important operating and customer asset.

rationales.quote: Is there an upper limit on city complexity or city size you could support today?
rationales.explanation: He tests the current operational scalability of the product across larger or more complex cities.

rationales.quote: Like who owns what
rationales.explanation: Charles identifies ownership and company-hygiene checks as part of the investment diligence condition.

question is queried/neutral, not a negative belief. Greetings, jokes, biography, simple confirmations and bare In/Out without

Retain each distinct rationale-bearing target utterance and exact evidence turn. Multiple labels on a turn are allowed only
when distinct concepts are expressed. For a repeated concept in different substantive turns retain each occurrence.
Quotes must be exact nonempty substrings of that turn's attributed_text, never continuation narration or another speaker.
The full text is included for context, but only attributed_text is eligible quote evidence.

post-pitch interviews, later diligence and subsequent updates; teaser is an opening preview/repeated future clip. Use unclear
when timing is uncertain. Do not use the redacted input cutoff as the end of original in-room discussion. Same-session
reversals stay original_pitch. Do not mix retrospective opinions into original-pitch scoring.

merely any question. decision_link supports_in/out ONLY if the target links the rationale to the commitment/refusal.
Confidence concerns the annotation, not investment probability. Return reviewed_target_turns containing EVERY supplied target
turn index exactly once, even when it contains no rationale. An empty rationale list is valid if none was expressed.
Be concise: prefer one short exact quote per distinct concept/turn, and a one-sentence explanation. Never claim human validation.
